# Drawbore

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/README.md

# Drawbore

> Composable agents that hold by construction.

Drawbore is a Python SDK for building constrained, composable agent pipelines
with safety guarantees baked in as architecture — for high-stakes, deterministic
workflows in fintech, healthcare, legal, compliance, and beyond.

The thesis: **capability is a liability in high-stakes workflows; constraint is
the feature.** You compose tightly scoped, typed, schema-enforced, audit-logged
agents; the framework enforces the contracts and you write the business logic.

## Install

```bash
pip install drawbore            # core
pip install "drawbore[mcp]"     # + MCP server tools
pip install "drawbore[otlp]"    # + OTLP span export
```

## Sixty seconds

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from drawbore import agent, Pipeline

class Payment(BaseModel):
    cents: int

class Normalized(BaseModel):
    dollars: float

@agent(name="normalize", input=Payment, output=Normalized)
async def normalize(p: Payment) -> Normalized:
    return Normalized(dollars=p.cents / 100)

pipeline = Pipeline(name="payments", version="1.0.0")
pipeline.add(normalize)

async def main():
    async with pipeline.test_mode() as tp:
        result = await tp.run(Payment(cents=2500))
    assert result.status == "completed"
    print(result.audit_trace.legible())   # a regulator-readable run record
```

Every step is schema-checked at both edges. Every tool call passes through a
proxy with a single-use permission token. Every run produces a legible audit
record. None of it is configurable off.

## What the framework guarantees

- **Typed contracts at every edge** — Pydantic-validated inputs and outputs;
  a wrong shape halts the run with a readable reason, it never propagates.
- **Least-privilege tools** — agents call only the tools they declared, through
  one audited chokepoint, with single-use scoped tokens and circuit breakers.
- **Halt-and-escalate by default** — failures stop the pipeline and produce an
  escalation package a human can read; there is no silent degradation.
- **Audit as a side effect** — `result.audit_trace.legible()` renders what ran,
  what was called, and why it stopped, with no tracing setup.
- **Test mode with the real safety layer** — `pipeline.test_mode(...)` mocks the
  outside world (models, tools, MCP) while every control runs for real.

## Learn more

- [Quickstart](docs/quickstart.mdx) — install to first run.
- [Guides](docs/guide/) — pipelines, tools, model-backed agents, escalation,
  testing, observability.
- [Examples](examples/) — runnable, tested pipelines from tiny to high-stakes.

# common-mistakes.mdx

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/agents/common-mistakes.mdx

title: "Common mistakes"
description: "Mistakes coding agents make with Drawbore, and the correct pattern for each."

Each entry names a mistake and the correct approach.

### Catching validation errors to "keep going"
Wrong: wrapping a step in try/except to swallow a schema violation. Right: let the
boundary halt; fix the data or the schema. Drawbore halts on purpose.

### Calling a tool that wasn't declared
Wrong: invoking a tool the agent didn't list. Right: declare it in
`@agent(tools=[...])`; the proxy blocks undeclared calls.

### Relying on implicit data flow for fan-in
Wrong: assuming a later step automatically sees an earlier step's output. Right:
use `From("agent.field")` bindings on every fan-in branch. A branch added with no
`inputs=` takes its input from the immediately preceding step in declaration order
— in a fan-in topology that is a sibling branch, not the fork. An omitted binding
surfaces at run time as a `schema_violation` halt naming the branch's input schema.
See [Pipelines — Binding inputs in fan-in topologies](/docs/guide/pipelines).

### Putting provider keys in pipeline JSON
Wrong: serializing credentials or a gateway into the manifest. Right: keep
`model="profile:..."` in the manifest; configure providers in the runtime LLM
config. See [Model-backed agents](/docs/guide/model-backed-agents).

### Testing against live models or tools
Wrong: hitting a real provider in tests. Right: use `pipeline.test_mode(...)` with
mocked models and tools — the safety layer runs for real. See
[Testing Drawbore](/docs/agents/testing-drawbore).

### Producing partial results on failure
Wrong: returning a half-finished result on failure. Right: let the run halt and
escalate — Drawbore has no partial-results mode; a halted run's `halt_code` and
escalation package tell a human exactly what stopped and why.

### Wrapping framework-registered handlers to time or log them
Wrong: wrapping an MCP or builtin tool handler after registration to capture
timing or a log entry. Right: the proxy already records every call — read
`result.metrics.tool_calls` for per-call tool, operation, duration, and
disposition. See [Tools — Instrumenting and observing tool calls](/guide/tools).

---

# context7.mdx

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/agents/context7.mdx

title: "Retrieving Drawbore docs with Context7"
description: "How a coding agent fetches current Drawbore documentation through Context7 and llms.txt."

Drawbore publishes its public documentation for retrieval. A coding agent can pull
current docs through Context7 or the site's `llms.txt`, rather than relying on
training data.

## When to use this

Before writing Drawbore code, fetch the current guides and reference so you use the
documented public APIs and the latest patterns.

## How

- **Context7:** resolve the Drawbore library, then query the docs for the topic you
  need (e.g. "pipeline.test_mode usage", "From bindings", "model profiles").
- **llms.txt:** the docs site exposes `llms.txt` / `llms-full.txt` listing the
  public pages; fetch the page whose title matches your topic.

Each public page states its topic in the title, says when to use it in the first
paragraph, and names common mistakes — so a retrieved page is usable on its own.

Prefer the documented public APIs shown in the [guides](/docs/guide/pipelines) and
examples.

---

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/agents/index.mdx

title: "Drawbore for coding agents"
description: "How a coding agent in a consumer repository should use Drawbore correctly."

This section is for **coding agents working in a user's application repository**
after Drawbore is installed. If you are an agent generating Drawbore code, read
these pages before writing a pipeline.

Drawbore's public APIs are the contract. Prefer the patterns shown in the
[guides](/docs/guide/pipelines) and examples over inventing your own.

## Pages

- [Rules](/docs/agents/rules) — the short, load-bearing rules to follow.
- [Common mistakes](/docs/agents/common-mistakes) — what agents get wrong and the
  correct pattern.
- [Testing Drawbore](/docs/agents/testing-drawbore) — write tests with
  `pipeline.test_mode(...)`.
- [Context7](/docs/agents/context7) — retrieve current Drawbore docs.

These pages link to the same human-facing guides and reference; they are not a
separate source of truth.

# rules.mdx

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/agents/rules.mdx

title: "Rules for using Drawbore"
description: "The load-bearing rules a coding agent should follow when writing Drawbore pipelines."

Follow these when writing Drawbore code. They mirror the framework's guarantees;
breaking them usually means fighting the framework.

1. **Define typed inputs and outputs.** Every agent takes a Pydantic model and
   returns one. Let validation halt on a wrong shape — do not catch and continue.
2. **Use explicit `From(...)` bindings** when a step consumes fields from an
   earlier step. Do not rely on implicit predecessor passing for fan-in.
3. **Declare every tool.** An agent may only call tools listed in
   `@agent(tools=[...])`. Tool calls route through the proxy — never call a tool
   handler directly.
4. **Let it halt.** Halt-and-escalate is the only failure behavior. Do not catch
   a halt to fabricate a partial result — read `RunResult.halt_code`, fix the
   cause or escalate to a human.
5. **Test with `pipeline.test_mode(...)`.** Mock models, tools, MCP servers, and
   external APIs there; the real safety layer still runs. See
   [Testing Drawbore](/docs/agents/testing-drawbore).
6. **Treat pipeline JSON as shape and policy**, not as runtime credentials or live
   objects. Provider/model config lives in the runtime LLM config, not the
   manifest.
7. **Assert on `RunResult` and `audit_trace`** when testing behaviour.

For the full rationale, read the [guides](/docs/guide/pipelines).

---

# testing-drawbore.mdx

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/agents/testing-drawbore.mdx

title: "Testing Drawbore pipelines"
description: "Write tests with pipeline.test_mode — mock the outside world while every safety control runs for real."

Use `pipeline.test_mode(...)` to test a pipeline locally. It mocks models, tools,
MCP servers, and external APIs while the real Drawbore safety layer (schema
validation, the tool proxy, halt-and-escalate, audit) runs unchanged.

## When to use this

Always, for pipeline tests. Never call a live provider or external service in a
unit test — a missing mock fails closed with a clear error rather than reaching
the network.

## Pattern

```python
async with pipeline.test_mode(
    mock_model_responses={"scorer": {"risk": "low"}},
    mock_tools={"transactions_db.read_transaction": {"amount": 100}},
) as tp:
    result = await tp.run(Initial(...))
    assert result.status == "completed"
    assert "low" in result.audit_trace.legible()
```

Assert on `result.status`, the typed final output, and `result.audit_trace`.

See the [Local testing guide](/docs/guide/local-testing) for the full surface
(loop scripts, evidence stores, escalation, and fallback).

---

# agentic-tool-loop.mdx

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/guide/agentic-tool-loop.mdx

title: "Agentic tool loop: let the model use tools, safely"
description: "A model-backed agent that declares tools can call them mid-completion — every call through the proxy and a one-time token, any failure halts, the loop is bounded, and Drawbore validates the final answer."

A model-backed agent can do more than one shot. When it **declares tools**,
Drawbore runs it as a bounded tool loop: the model calls a tool, sees the result,
and continues — until it returns a final answer that Drawbore validates against the
agent's output schema. The orchestration engine is hidden; you write an ordinary
agent.

```python
from drawbore import Pipeline, agent
from drawbore.orchestration import ADKEngine
from drawbore.llm import LLMRuntime, LLMRuntimeConfig, ModelProfile, ModelTarget, ProviderConfig

@agent(name="screen", input=Transactions, output=Verdict, model="gpt-4o", tools=["risk_lookup"])
async def screen(txns, tools):
    ...  # the function body is not run on the model path

runtime = LLMRuntime(config=LLMRuntimeConfig(
    profiles={"default": ModelProfile(targets=(
        ModelTarget(provider="openai", model="gpt-4o"),
    ))},
    providers={"openai": ProviderConfig(credential_env="OPENAI_API_KEY")},
))

p = Pipeline(name="aml", registry=registry)
p.add(screen)
result = await p.run(transactions, engine=ADKEngine(llm_runtime=runtime))
```

Every tool call the model makes goes through the same proxy and single-use token as
any other Drawbore tool — only the agent's *declared* tools exist, and the call is
traced and audited. The model never gets to route around a control:

- **Any tool failure or denial halts** the step and escalates with a legible reason
  — the loop does not "recover" around a tripped control. A proxy denial keeps its own
  halt code (for example `taint_violation` when the
  [taint breaker](/guide/taint-and-trust) refuses an exfil-capable call, `token_violation`,
  or `circuit_breaker`).
- **The loop is bounded** (`max_llm_calls`, default 8) — a runaway loop halts.
- **Drawbore owns the answer** — the model's final output is parsed and validated
  against your output model. A model that declares tools cannot be pinned to JSON-only
  output on its final turn (forcing structured output and offering tools are mutually
  exclusive), so a model that narrates before answering may wrap its JSON in prose. If
  the final answer holds exactly one top-level JSON object, Drawbore extracts it
  deterministically and the step proceeds — a pure re-parse of what the model already
  said, so no tool is re-invoked.
- **A stuck turn earns one reprompt.** A loop turn passes through the same
  [structured-output boundary](/guide/production-llm-gateway) as a one-shot answer.
  Sometimes a model returns prose describing what it intends to do ("I will call
  `lookup` with …") instead of emitting a structured tool call, or returns prose with no
  usable JSON answer. Drawbore never parses or executes a tool out of that prose — a tool
  runs only when the model emits a real structured call. Instead it reprompts the
  **same** model **once** on the same session, asking it to respond with either a
  structured tool call or a single JSON answer and nothing else; the corrected turn then
  continues the normal loop. The reprompt is a pure model turn (it counts against
  `max_llm_calls` and never replays a tool side effect) and happens **at most once per
  stuck turn**.
- **A final answer that misses your schema earns the same one reprompt.** When the
  final answer parses as a JSON object but fails the agent's output schema (for example a
  missing required field), Drawbore reprompts **once** — seeded with the exact field
  errors — before halting. If the corrected answer is still schema-invalid, the step
  halts `schema_violation` (the schema gate is never weakened — you get one corrective
  chance, then it stands). This reprompt shares the single per-turn budget with the
  prose case above: a turn never gets two reprompts.

When a reprompt happens it is visible on the audit trail: `RunResult`'s `audit_trace`
records a per-step `reprompts` count (`0` or `1`), and the step's `invoke_agent` span
carries `drawbore.structured_output.reprompts`.

The loop side of the recovered-vs-halted contract:

| Model behaviour | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Valid JSON object matching your schema | Accepted. |
| A single JSON object wrapped in prose | **Recovered** deterministically (no extra model call). |
| Prose with no usable tool call or JSON answer (a *narrated* tool call) | **Recovered** via one bounded reprompt, if it then yields a structured call or a JSON object; the narrated call is **never** executed. |
| A JSON object that fails your output schema | **Recovered** via one bounded reprompt seeded with the field errors, if the corrected answer matches; otherwise **halted** `schema_violation`. |
| Valid JSON that is **not** an object (array/scalar) | **Halted** immediately (`model_error`), no reprompt. |
| Zero or still-ambiguous (more than one) objects **after** the one reprompt | **Halted** (`model_error`) with a bounded excerpt; Drawbore never guesses which object to trust. |
| No model budget (`max_llm_calls`) remaining | **Halted** without reprompting. |

The number of model turns and every tool call are in the audit trail:

```python
step = result.audit_trace.step_records[0]
print(step.model_turns)   # e.g. 3
print(step.tool_calls)    # ('risk_lookup (invoke) -> ok', ...)
```

A tool ref the model cannot name verbatim still works. Function-calling providers
restrict a tool's name to letters, digits, `_`, and `-`, so a ref like
`mcp://sanctions_feed/latest_updates` or `evidence://retrieve` cannot be sent as-is.
Drawbore exposes each such tool to the model under a provider-safe alias and resolves
the alias the model picks back to the canonical ref before the call runs. You keep
writing the canonical ref; scope enforcement, the one-time token, the proxy log, and
the audit trail all stay keyed on the canonical ref (the alias is only the name the
provider sees).

The loop only ever offers the model the agent's *declared* tools. A call to anything else —
an invented alias that maps to no declared tool, or a tool that is registered but not declared
by this agent — never reaches the proxy, so it does not produce a proxy scope denial. It fails
closed at the model boundary and halts `model_error`. (A deterministic agent that calls a
registered-but-undeclared tool directly halts `tool_access` instead — same fail-closed outcome,
different halt code.) For loop steps, alert on `model_error` for this case; see
[Taint and trust](/guide/taint-and-trust) for how the breaker's `taint_violation` carries over
to loop-invoked tools, and [Branching on a halt](/guide/reliability#branching-on-a-halt) for the
full vocabulary.

This composes with evidence compression: a compressed step's model can retrieve the
full original mid-loop with the `evidence://retrieve` tool — scoped by the proxy, a
handle is not authority.

You supply a model-capable engine (today, `ADKEngine`). A model-backed agent run on
an engine with no model path fails closed with a legible error. Model fallback
inside the loop, streaming, and parallel tool calls in one turn are not in Phase 1
(a loop agent uses its primary model; declaring `fallback_model` fails closed).

---

# base_manifest agent 'payment_validator' field 'ref':

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/guide/authority-regression.mdx

title: "Authority regression checks"
description: "Fail CI when a pipeline edit grants an agent new tool or evidence authority."

**When to use this:** you want a CI gate that blocks a pipeline change if it lets an
agent reach a tool or evidence scope it could not reach before — the agent equivalent of
"prove this policy change grants no new access."

Drawbore can compute this because a pipeline's authority is *declared*: the serialized
manifest plus the single-use capability tokens the proxy mints. From a manifest it derives
a **capability footprint** — the set of `(agent, tool/evidence, ref, scope)` facts the
pipeline may exercise — and diffs two footprints.

```python
from drawbore.config import PipelineConfig, check_no_new_authority
from drawbore.config.errors import AuthorityRegressionError

old = PipelineConfig.model_validate(base_manifest)
new = PipelineConfig.model_validate(head_manifest)
try:
    check_no_new_authority(old, new)        # raises if the new manifest grants more
except AuthorityRegressionError as exc:
    print(exc)                              # a regulator-legible certificate
    raise
```

**What counts as new authority (v1):** an added tool on any agent, or any evidence-retrieval
grant newly given to an agent (a new `search` or `full` scope, or an existing policy newly
enabled). The check is *sound but coarse* — it ignores branch
conditions (worst-case reachable) and tool operations, so it never misses an expansion but
cannot credit a narrowing achieved purely by tightening a branch.

If you want the raw diff rather than a raised exception, call `authority_diff` directly:

```python
from drawbore.config import authority_diff

diff = authority_diff(old, new)
if not diff.ok:
    print(diff.certificate())   # same human-readable + JSON payload the error carries
```

The certificate includes the footprint fingerprints of both manifests — paste them into a
PR comment as a reproducible provenance anchor.

To verify that a running pipeline stayed within its declared footprint, use the
`test_mode` soundness helper:

```python
from drawbore.testing import assert_footprint_sound

async with pipeline.test_mode(...) as tp:
    result = await tp.run(payload)

assert_footprint_sound(config, result.audit_trace)
```

`assert_footprint_sound` reads `RunResult.audit_trace` — the same audit record available
in production — and raises `AssertionError` if any tool or evidence ref the run exercised
is absent from the manifest's static footprint. Run it in your acceptance tests to catch
the day a future change binds a ref the manifest cannot see.

See the full runnable CI-gate example at `examples/authority_regression_ci.py`.

## Input-schema relaxation

A second monotonicity check on the _data_ axis: where authority monotonicity asks
"did this agent gain a new _capability_?", the schema-relaxation oracle asks
"did this agent's _input gate_ get weaker?" A relaxation is any schema change that
makes an agent accept a strictly wider set of inputs — a raised `maxLength`, a
dropped `required` field, a widened `enum`, a loosened numeric bound, a removed
`pattern` or `type` constraint. A weaker input gate is a safety regression even
when no capability changes: the validation that used to reject malformed data no
longer does.

`check_no_schema_relaxation(old, new)` checks every agent present in _both_
manifests, matched by name:

```python
from drawbore.config import PipelineConfig, check_no_schema_relaxation
from drawbore.config.errors import SchemaRelaxationError

old = PipelineConfig.model_validate(base_manifest)
new = PipelineConfig.model_validate(head_manifest)
try:
    check_no_schema_relaxation(old, new)     # raises if any agent's input schema relaxed
except SchemaRelaxationError as exc:
    print(exc.diff.legible())                # regulator-readable certificate
    raise
```

Catching a `maxLength` relaxation (the most common kind):

```python
# base_manifest agent 'payment_validator' field 'ref':
#   {"type": "string", "maxLength": 12}
# head_manifest agent 'payment_validator' field 'ref':
#   {"type": "string", "maxLength": 50}

check_no_schema_relaxation(old_config, new_config)
# raises SchemaRelaxationError — legible() output:
#   Input-schema relaxation check: FAILED — 1 relaxation(s) detected.
#   - agent 'payment_validator' at /properties/ref/maxLength: 'maxLength' relaxed
#     (old=12 -> new=50); upper bound raised; larger values now accepted
```

For the raw diff without raising:

```python
from drawbore.config import schema_relaxation_diff

diff = schema_relaxation_diff(old, new)
if not diff.ok:
    print(diff.legible())   # same certificate the error carries
```

`SchemaRelaxationDiff.legible()` includes the SHA-256 fingerprints of both
manifests' input-schema maps — suitable as a provenance anchor in a PR comment or
audit record.

**Fail-closed honesty clause.** The oracle's contract is _sound, not complete_: it
never passes a genuine relaxation, and it fails closed (flags) on any change it
cannot prove is a narrowing. Regex (`pattern`), structural keywords (`anyOf`,
`oneOf`, `allOf`, `type`, `$ref`), and any non-metadata keyword removal always
flag — even when the specific change is semantically safe. The only keyword
removals that are silently allowed are the pure-annotation set: `title`,
`description`, `default`, and `examples`. If the oracle flags a change you believe
is correct, the right response is human review; bypassing the check is not.

**Toolchain-version caveat.** The input schema is captured from `model_json_schema()`
at `to_config()` export time. Comparing manifests produced under different Pydantic
minor versions can surface version-artifact "relaxations" that are not real
behavioral changes — the oracle flags them fail-closed (never a false-pass). Pin
your Pydantic version across baseline and candidate builds to eliminate
version-artifact noise.

**Known limitation: matching is by agent name.** An agent present in one manifest
but absent from the other is skipped — added and removed agents are the authority
diff's concern. A relaxation on an agent that was _renamed_ between versions is not
caught here. However, if the renamed agent carried tool declarations, the authority
monotonicity check will flag the new name as gaining new authority and hold the
candidate for human review before the schema check would run.

If you use the self-improvement admission gate (`drawbore.ratchet.admit()`), this
check runs automatically as a second monotonicity layer alongside the capability-
authority check. A candidate that relaxes any agent's input schema yields
`verdict.admitted = False`, `verdict.schema_diff` carries the diff, and
`verdict.legible()` renders it for a reviewer. See
[Safety ratchet](/docs/guide/safety-ratchet).

### API reference

**`check_no_schema_relaxation(old: PipelineConfig, new: PipelineConfig) -> None`**

Raises `SchemaRelaxationError` if any name-matched agent's input schema was
relaxed; returns `None` on identity or a pure tightening. Admission and CI use
only — never raised by the pipeline runtime.

**`schema_relaxation_diff(old: PipelineConfig, new: PipelineConfig) -> SchemaRelaxationDiff`**

Returns the raw diff without raising. `diff.ok` is `True` when no relaxation was
found; `diff.relaxations` is a tuple of `SchemaRelaxation` items when not.

**`SchemaRelaxation`**

One flagged relaxation at a concrete JSON-schema path. Fields: `agent` (matched
agent name), `path` (e.g. `/properties/ref/maxLength`), `keyword` (the
JSON-schema keyword involved), `old`/`new` (old and new values; `None` when
absent), `reason` (auditor-readable one-liner).

**`SchemaRelaxationDiff`**

The full comparison result. `ok` is `True` iff `relaxations` is empty.
`old_fingerprint`/`new_fingerprint` are SHA-256 fingerprints of the input-schema
maps of both manifests. `legible()` returns a human-readable certificate (also
aliased as `certificate()` for uniform integration with the ratchet verdict).

**`SchemaRelaxationError`**

Raised by `check_no_schema_relaxation`. `.diff` holds the `SchemaRelaxationDiff`
for structured inspection. A plain `Exception` (not a `DrawboreError`): this check
runs at admission/CI time only and is not part of the pipeline runtime halt-code
vocabulary.

---

# confinement-receipt.mdx

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/guide/confinement-receipt.mdx

title: "Confinement receipt"
description: "An offline, independently-verifiable attestation that a run stayed within its declared tool authority and never exfiltrated under untrusted data."

**When to use this:** you need to demonstrate to a regulator, auditor, or compliance
team that a specific run was confined — not because you trust the runtime's logs, but
because the claim can be checked independently, without re-running the pipeline and
without trusting Drawbore. A `ConfinementReceipt` is proof, not logs or inference.

A receipt is minted automatically at the end of **every** run — success or halt. It
binds the pipeline's declared capability footprint (the set of `(agent, tool, scope)`
facts the run was allowed to exercise) to the proxy's observed enforcement log and
re-checks both confinement invariants offline.

## Quick example

```python
import asyncio
from drawbore.confinement import verify

result = await pipeline.run(initial)

receipt = result.confinement_receipt
verdict = verify(receipt)
print(verdict.status)          # "confined" | "breached" | "unverifiable"
print(receipt.legible())       # regulator-readable block
```

To bind the receipt to the actual execution log, pass the proxy log as a second
argument. Each log entry's `run_id` is also checked against the receipt's `run_id`,
so a different run's log with otherwise identical calls is rejected:

```python
verdict = verify(receipt, result.proxy_log)
print(verdict.status)          # re-derives the verdict from the live log
```

To bind the declared footprint to the manifest fingerprint you hold independently
(the strongest defence against inflated `declared_facts`), pass it as a keyword
argument:

```python
from drawbore.config.authority import effective_authority

config = pipeline.to_config()
expected_fp = effective_authority(config).fingerprint()
verdict = verify(receipt, expected_footprint_fingerprint=expected_fp)
```

## The three verdict statuses

`verify` returns a `ConfinementVerdict` with a `status` field:

- **`confined`** — every executed tool call mapped to a declared capability, and no
  exfil-capable tool fired under untrusted data. The run was contained.
- **`breached`** — at least one executed call fell outside the declared footprint, or
  an exfil-capable tool ran under an untrusted taint scope. `verdict.breaches` names
  each offending call.
- **`unverifiable`** — the evidence is insufficient to prove containment. Possible
  causes: the footprint could not be derived, a tool call could not be attributed to
  an agent, or the receipt's fingerprint does not match. Fail closed: insufficient
  evidence is never treated as confined.

Verdict precedence is `unverifiable > breached > confined`. A `denied:*` proxy entry
(a scope denial, taint denial, token denial, or circuit-breaker trip) is **not** a
breach — it is evidence a control fired, which strengthens the proof.

## What `verify` proves — and what it does not

`verify` offers layered tamper-detection; each layer has an honest scope.

**`verify(receipt)`** re-derives the receipt's SHA-256 fingerprint from its
embedded fields and re-evaluates the confinement invariants over the embedded
observed calls. It detects edits that did NOT recompute the keyless fingerprint.
It also checks that `receipt.footprint_fingerprint` is consistent with
`receipt.declared_facts`, catching a forger who changed one without updating the
other. It does NOT detect a fully self-consistent forgery: an adversary who
rewrites `declared_facts`, recomputes `footprint_fingerprint` over the new facts,
and recomputes `receipt_fingerprint` over all fields produces a receipt that passes
`verify(receipt)` alone — because the SHA-256 algorithm is public and keyless.

**`verify(receipt, proxy_log)`** additionally re-derives the observed calls from
the live proxy log and asserts they equal the embedded calls. Each log entry's
`run_id` is checked against `receipt.run_id`, so a different run's log with
byte-identical calls is rejected. This proves **log binding**: the receipt matches
the actual execution, not a substituted or redacted log.

**`verify(receipt, expected_footprint_fingerprint=fp)`** additionally asserts that
`receipt.footprint_fingerprint` equals the fingerprint the auditor holds
independently (computed from the pipeline manifest via
`effective_authority(config).fingerprint()`). This closes the self-consistent
forgery gap: even if an adversary inflates `declared_facts` and recomputes all
keyless fingerprints consistently, the inflated footprint will not match the
manifest fingerprint derived independently.

The independence is verifier-vs-runtime: an auditor re-derives the verdict from the
evidence using the same deterministic rules that minted it, without trusting the
runtime and without re-running the pipeline. This is the regulatory value of the
receipt.

## Honesty clause

The receipt is **verifiable, not cryptographically signed**. The SHA-256
fingerprint is keyless: it detects naive tampering and internal inconsistencies
(such as a `footprint_fingerprint` that does not match its `declared_facts`), but
an adversary who knows the SHA-256 algorithm — which is public — can rewrite every
field and recompute every fingerprint to produce a self-consistent receipt that
passes `verify(receipt)` alone. Full forgery and repudiation resistance require
cryptographic signing (Ed25519), which is a managed-service feature, not part of
the MIT core.

For audit purposes, use `verify(receipt, proxy_log, expected_footprint_fingerprint=fp)`:
binding to both the live execution log and the independently-held manifest
fingerprint closes the gap that keyless SHA-256 alone leaves open.

For a correctly-functioning runtime the verdict is always `confined` — the proxy
already prevents out-of-footprint and exfil-under-untrusted-scope calls. `breached`
surfaces a runtime defect or tampering; that is exactly what a regulatory attestation
is meant to catch.

## `run_id` and per-run identity

`ConfinementReceipt.run_id` comes from the `run_id` you pass to `pipeline.run()`.
If you do not pass one, it defaults to a non-unique `"<pipeline-name>-run"`. Pass an
explicit unique identifier (a UUID, a request id, a job id) so each receipt has an
independent, addressable identity:

```python
import uuid
result = await pipeline.run(initial, run_id=str(uuid.uuid4()))
```

## Distinguishing the two `status` fields

`ConfinementReceipt` and `ConfinementVerdict` each have a `status` field; they mean
different things:

- `ConfinementReceipt.status` — the **run** outcome: `"completed"`, `"halted"`, or
  `"escalated"`.
- `ConfinementVerdict.status` — the **confinement** verdict: `"confined"`,
  `"breached"`, or `"unverifiable"`.

A halted run (for example, a schema violation) produces a receipt with
`status="halted"` and can still have `verdict.status="confined"` if the tool calls
that did execute stayed within the declared footprint.

## API reference

**`ConfinementReceipt`** — the self-contained attestation artifact on
`RunResult.confinement_receipt`. Always present. Fields: `run_id`, `status`
(run status), `footprint_fingerprint` (SHA-256 of the declared capability facts),
`declared_facts`, `step_agents`, `observed_calls`, `verdict`, `receipt_fingerprint`.
Call `.legible()` for a regulator-readable, single-block account.

**`ObservedCall`** — one proxy-log entry as the receipt records it. Fields: `step`,
`agent`, `tool_ref`, `operation`, `match_kind` (`"tool"` / `"evidence"` / `None`),
`result`, `taint_scope`, `exfil_capable`, `input_hash`, `output_hash`.
`match_kind` is for legibility only; confinement matching is on `(agent, tool_ref)`.

**`ConfinementVerdict`** — the confinement outcome. Fields: `status`
(`"confined"` / `"breached"` / `"unverifiable"`), `confined` (bool, always equals
`status == "confined"`), `breaches` (tuple of strings naming each breach),
`unverifiable` (tuple of strings naming each unverifiable reason).

**`verify(receipt, proxy_log=None, *, expected_footprint_fingerprint=None) -> ConfinementVerdict`** — offline verifier.
Never raises; returns `unverifiable` on any error. Import from `drawbore.confinement`.

- `proxy_log` — when provided, re-derives observed calls from the live log and
  checks each entry's `run_id` against `receipt.run_id`.
- `expected_footprint_fingerprint` — when provided, asserts that
  `receipt.footprint_fingerprint` equals this value (e.g. from
  `effective_authority(config).fingerprint()`), closing the self-consistent
  keyless-forgery gap.

```python
from drawbore.confinement import verify
```

For the declared capability footprint that the receipt checks against, see
[Authority regression checks](/guide/authority-regression).
For the taint invariant the receipt binds to observed enforcement, see
[Taint and trust](/guide/taint-and-trust).

---

# First process: runs until it halts, persisting each completed step.

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/guide/durable-resume.mdx

title: "Durable resume"
description: "Resume a checkpointed run safely — and refuse the resume when the pipeline changed underneath it."

Use durable resume when a pipeline run can halt partway (a model outage, an
escalation, a crash) and you want to continue it later without re-executing
the steps that already succeeded. Drawbore's resume is refuse-on-drift: before
restoring anything, the runtime verifies that the pipeline still means what it
meant when the checkpoint was taken. If an agent's declared contract or the
pipeline's topology changed, the resume halts with `halt_code ==
"resume_drift"` instead of replaying outputs into changed logic — and it halts
before executing a single step.

## Resuming a run

Pass a checkpoint store and a stable `run_id`:

```python
from drawbore.state import InMemoryCheckpointStore

store = InMemoryCheckpointStore()
first = await pipeline.run(order, run_id="order-A-1", checkpoints=store)   # halts at step 3
again = await pipeline.run(order, run_id="order-A-1", checkpoints=store)  # resumes at step 3
```

Completed steps are restored from the store, not re-executed. Each completed
step also records a **seal** — a snapshot of the agent's declared contract
(version, risk tier, tools, model, fallback model, instructions, input/output
schemas, approval requirement, and the step's evidence policy).

## Resuming across a process restart

`InMemoryCheckpointStore` lives only for the lifetime of the process, so it
resumes within one run of your program. To resume after the process exits — a
worker that crashes and restarts, a job picked up by a different machine — use
`FileCheckpointStore`, which persists the full checkpoint (outputs, skip marks,
topology fingerprint, seals, and trust labels) to a directory:

```python
from drawbore.state import FileCheckpointStore

# First process: runs until it halts, persisting each completed step.
store = FileCheckpointStore("/var/lib/myapp/checkpoints")
first = await pipeline.run(order, run_id="order-A-1", checkpoints=store)

# A later process (a restart): a brand-new store over the same directory
# restores the completed steps and resumes — no re-execution, no spurious drift.
store = FileCheckpointStore("/var/lib/myapp/checkpoints")
again = await pipeline.run(order, run_id="order-A-1", checkpoints=store)
```

Each step is written atomically (write a temp file, then rename), so a crash
mid-write never leaves a torn checkpoint: the previous committed step stays
intact and a half-written file is ignored on the next read.

Outputs are stored as plain field data, not a Python class path. On resume the
store rebuilds each typed output from the *live* pipeline's output schema for
that step, so a tampered checkpoint file can never make the store import an
arbitrary type. (This is why the same pipeline, with matching declarations,
must be rebuilt before you resume — exactly what the seal also verifies.)

## When resume says no

On resume, every stored seal is re-verified against the live pipeline before
anything runs. A mismatch refuses the whole resume:

```python
# Between attempts, someone changed the writer's model...
result = await pipeline.run(order, run_id="order-A-1", checkpoints=store)
assert result.status == "halted"
assert result.halt_code == "resume_drift"
print(result.reason)
# resume_drift: step 'confirmation_writer' changed since checkpoint (model); refusing to resume
```

Refusal is pre-flight: zero steps execute, so a refused resume has zero side
effects and never double-fires a completed step. Topology changes (steps
added, removed, or rewired) refuse the same way when the run had prior
progress; a `run_id` that never completed any step simply starts fresh.

## The resume ledger

Every run result carries `resume_ledger` — a regulator-readable record of what
the runtime observed:

```python
print(result.resume_ledger.legible())
# Run 'order-A-1': resumed from checkpointed state.
# Step 2 'confirmation_writer': resume refused — changed since checkpoint (model).
# 2 completed step(s) verified clean; resume was refused before any restore.
```

Each entry names the step, its disposition (`executed`, `restored`, `skipped`,
or `refused`), and the seal verdict. Branch on `halt_code`, never on the prose
(see [Reliability](/guide/reliability)).

## What the seal does and does not cover

The seal covers **declared** semantics. It does not fingerprint Python
function bodies: changing an agent's implementation without bumping `version`
is invisible to the seal. Bump `version` on any behavior change — that is the
author's half of the contract.

Two more boundaries to know:

- **Concurrent resumes are not serialized.** Two workers resuming the same
  `run_id` at the same time both pass verification and both execute. The seal
  refuses drifted resumes; it does not make execution single-use.
- **Custom checkpoint stores must persist seals.** `FileCheckpointStore`
  already does; if you write your own store, a store that implements only the
  older interface restores outputs but returns no seals, and an unverifiable
  step refuses the resume with `resume_drift` until the store implements
  `record_seal`/`seal_of`. Implement both together, and persist a step's
  output, trust, and seal atomically. Checkpoints written before seals existed
  also refuse with `resume_drift`: re-run those flows fresh under a new
  `run_id`.

## Exactly-once effects

Checkpointing resumes at the first incomplete step. But what about a step that
had already fired some effectful tool calls — a charge, a notification, an
external write — before the crash? Without extra bookkeeping, those calls would
fire again.

The **effect ledger** solves this. When a step resumes, each effectful tool call
is replayed from the ledger instead of being re-fired: the recorded output is
returned, and the real handler is never called a second time.

### Mark tools as effectful or read-only

Every tool defaults to `effectful=True` — the fail-closed choice. An
unclassified tool is treated as effectful so it is never silently double-fired.
Mark pure read-only tools `effectful=False` so resume re-queries them live
instead of replaying a stale recorded result:

```python
registry.register_tool(
    "payments.charge",
    charge_handler,
    effectful=True,    # default; explicit for clarity
)
registry.register_tool(
    "records.read_customer",
    read_customer,
    effectful=False,   # safe to re-query; no ledger overhead
)
```

`effectful` is supported on `register_tool`, `register_builtin`, and
`register_mcp_tool`. The builtin `evidence://retrieve` is already registered
`effectful=False`.

### Wire the ledger alongside the checkpoint store

Pass an `effect_ledger` together with `checkpoints` and a fixed `run_id`:

```python
from drawbore.state import FileCheckpointStore, InMemoryEffectLedger

store = FileCheckpointStore("/var/lib/myapp/checkpoints")
ledger = InMemoryEffectLedger()

first = await pipeline.run(order, run_id="order-A-1", checkpoints=store, effect_ledger=ledger)
# process crashes partway...
again = await pipeline.run(order, run_id="order-A-1", checkpoints=store, effect_ledger=ledger)
# effectful calls already recorded are replayed, never re-fired
```

The same `effect_ledger=` kwarg works with `pipeline.test_mode(...).run(...)`.

### What happens on resume

For each effectful call in the resuming step the proxy looks up the position in
the ledger:

- **No entry found** — first-time execution; the handler is called normally and
  the result is recorded.
- **Entry found, `SUCCEEDED`** — the recorded output is returned; the handler
  is not called.
- **Entry found, `PENDING`** — the handler fired but the ledger's confirmation
  write was lost in the crash. The framework cannot prove the call succeeded
  exactly once, so it halts `effect_unresolved` fail-closed. The recorded
  idempotency key lets an operator verify the outcome against the remote system.
  Resolving a pending entry (clearing or voiding it) is not yet part of the
  public API; the run halts for human reconciliation.
- **Divergence** — a call at a recorded position does not match what was
  recorded (different tool or different arguments), or the resuming step fires
  fewer effectful calls than were recorded (skipping a previously-fired effect).
  The run halts `effect_divergence` rather than risk a double-fire or silent
  replay gap.

See [Reliability](/guide/reliability) for the full halt-code vocabulary.

### Deterministic steps vs. model-driven loops

The replay contract is strongest for **deterministic steps**: the same inputs
always produce the same tool-call sequence, so a resumed deterministic step
replays cleanly. Model-driven agentic loops are non-deterministic in call order:
a resumed loop either reproduces the recorded sequence exactly or halts
`effect_divergence` fail-closed. Design effectful agentic loops with that
trade-off in mind.

### Remote dedup with `current_idempotency_key()`

There is a one-window residual risk: the handler succeeds, but the process
crashes before the ledger records `SUCCEEDED`. On the next resume the ledger
finds `PENDING` and halts. For calls to remote systems that support idempotency
keys (Stripe, Adyen, most payment processors), you can push the dedup downstream
and close the window:

```python
from drawbore.tools import current_idempotency_key

async def charge_handler(args):
    key = current_idempotency_key()  # stable hex key, unique per run/step/position/tool
    return await stripe.charge(
        amount=args["amount"],
        idempotency_key=key,         # remote system deduplicates on its side
    )
```

`current_idempotency_key()` returns the key while inside an effectful tool call
and `None` outside one.

### Ledger types

All four types are exported from `drawbore.state`:

| Type | Role |
|------|------|
| `EffectLedger` | ABC — implement this for a durable backend |
| `InMemoryEffectLedger` | Default in-process implementation |
| `EffectEntry` | A single recorded call (`run_id`, `step`, `position`, `tool_ref`, `input_hash`, `idempotency_key`, `status`, `output`) |
| `EffectStatus` | `"pending"` or `"succeeded"` |

### Durable ledger backends

`InMemoryEffectLedger` does not survive process restart. For real
crash-and-resume across machine failures, implement `EffectLedger` with a
durable backend — a database row, a file, a cloud store. The interface mirrors
`CheckpointStore`: a small, synchronous ABC with `record_pending`,
`record_succeeded`, `entry_at`, `recorded_count`, and `entries_from`. All writes
must be durable before the method returns; async I/O must be bridged internally.

### Use `unclassified_effectful_tools()` as a CI check

```python
from drawbore.tools import unclassified_effectful_tools

unclassified = unclassified_effectful_tools(registry)
assert not unclassified, f"tools still at default effectful=True: {unclassified}"
```

This returns all tools currently marked effectful (the default), as candidates
to review and mark `effectful=False` if they are pure reads.

## Common mistakes

- **Reusing a `run_id` for a different request.** Resume is keyed by `run_id`;
  a reused id restores the previous run's outputs. Use one id per logical run.
- **Upgrading Pydantic mid-run.** Schema fingerprints can change across
  Pydantic minor versions, which reads as drift and refuses the resume. Safe,
  but plan upgrades between runs, not across them.
- **Treating `resume_drift` as retryable.** It is not transient. Either
  restore the pipeline to the checkpointed semantics, or start a fresh
  `run_id` under the new ones.
- **Passing a ledger without a checkpoint store.** The ledger and checkpoint
  store are complementary: the store skips already-completed steps; the ledger
  replays already-fired effects within a step. Neither alone prevents both
  classes of double-execution.
- **Using `InMemoryEffectLedger` across process restarts.** It does not
  persist. Use a durable backend if your resume must survive a process exit.

---

# the threshold lives on the pipeline; a RiskScore below it escalates

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/guide/escalation.mdx

title: "Escalation: putting a human in the loop"
description: "Hand a complete, readable package to a person when a run can't proceed safely."

A Drawbore run never guesses past a problem. When something blocks it — a failed
check, a low-confidence result, or a step marked as needing sign-off — it builds
an **escalation package** and hands it to a human.

## Attach a policy

```python
from drawbore import Pipeline
from drawbore.escalation import EscalationPolicy

pipeline = Pipeline(
    name="payments",
    on_failure=EscalationPolicy(channel="slack", target="compliance_queue", mode="sync"),
)
```

- **sync** — the run **stops and waits** for a person (use for irreversible actions).
- **async** — the run **flags and continues** (use for reviewable results, like audit).

`async` applies to the low-confidence trigger only. A failure or a step that
requires sign-off **always stops the run**, whatever the mode — there is no valid
result to carry forward.

## The package a human receives

Every escalation says which step stopped, what it received, what it tried to
produce, why it stopped, the steps completed before it, and when — readable
without an engineer.

```python
result = await pipeline.run(order)
if result.status == "escalated":
    print(result.escalations[-1].legible())
```

## Triggers

- **A failure** (schema, blocked tool, runaway loop, agent error) — always stops.
- **Low confidence** — mark an output model with `HasConfidence` and set a
  `confidence_threshold` on the pipeline; results below it escalate. Only marked
  models are checked — the framework never invents a confidence value.
- **Sign-off required** — declare `@agent(..., requires_human_approval=True)`; the
  step always stops for human approval.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from drawbore import Pipeline, agent
from drawbore.escalation import EscalationPolicy, HasConfidence

class RiskScore(BaseModel, HasConfidence):
    score: int
    confidence: float          # 0..1 — the framework never invents this

@agent(input=Order, output=RiskScore, requires_human_approval=True)
async def assess(order: Order) -> RiskScore:
    ...

# the threshold lives on the pipeline; a RiskScore below it escalates
pipeline = Pipeline(
    name="payments",
    on_failure=EscalationPolicy(channel="slack", target="compliance_queue"),
    confidence_threshold=0.80,
)
```

With no `on_failure` policy a failure still just halts (`status="halted"`). Real
delivery channels (Slack/email/webhook) and the approve/reject interface are part
of the managed service.

---

# evidence compressed (compressed for model); via json_rows; 4200->950 tokens; handle 8f3c...

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/guide/evidence-compression.mdx

title: "Evidence compression: give the model less, keep everything"
description: "Compress large evidence to a bounded, policy-approved view for a model-backed agent — the original is always retained and retrievable through the proxy, and every decision is audited."

High-stakes workflows carry large evidence: thousands of transactions, long logs,
hundreds of contract clauses. Drawbore lets a model-backed agent see a bounded,
policy-approved view of that evidence while keeping the original intact and every
compression and retrieval decision in the audit trail. Constraint, not blindness.

Compression is **opt-in** and **deterministic**: a step with no policy behaves
exactly as before, and the same input under the same policy always produces the
same bounded view.

## Turn it on for a step

```python
from drawbore import Pipeline
from drawbore.evidence import EvidencePolicy, InMemoryEvidenceStore

p = Pipeline(name="aml")
p.add(
    screen,                                   # a model-backed agent (@agent(model=...))
    evidence=EvidencePolicy(name="aml", enabled=True, min_tokens=800),
)

store = InMemoryEvidenceStore()
result = await p.run(transactions, engine=engine, evidence_store=store)
```

When the step's input is large enough, the framework compresses the evidence the
model sees (e.g. 2,000 transaction records → the high-signal rows plus a
representative sample), stores the full original, and records the decision:

```python
print(result.audit_trace.step_records[0].evidence)
# evidence compressed (compressed for model); via json_rows; 4200->950 tokens; handle 8f3c...
```

`enabled=False` (the default) is byte-identical passthrough. `mode="simulate"`
records what *would* be compressed without changing the payload — useful for
rolling the feature out safely.

## Retrieve the original, safely

The original is never lost. An agent that declares the evidence retrieval tool
can retrieve it through the proxy — scoped by a one-time token, gated by policy.

**Single wiring point.** Declare `EVIDENCE_TOOL_REF` in the agent's `tools=` and
pass `evidence_store=store` to `Pipeline.run` (or `test_mode`). That one argument
wires up both compression storage and retrieval — no separate
`register_evidence_tool` call needed:

```python
from drawbore.evidence import EVIDENCE_TOOL_REF, EvidencePolicy, InMemoryEvidenceStore

store = InMemoryEvidenceStore()

@agent(input=Transactions, output=Verdict, model="m", tools=[EVIDENCE_TOOL_REF])
async def screen(v, tools):
    hits = await tools.call(EVIDENCE_TOOL_REF, {"handle_id": h, "mode": "search", "query": "high_risk"})

p = Pipeline(name="aml")
p.add(screen, evidence=EvidencePolicy(name="aml", enabled=True, min_tokens=800))

result = await p.run(transactions, engine=engine, evidence_store=store)
```

The retrieval handler is bound to the exact same store used for compression, so
every handle your pipeline creates is immediately retrievable.

A handle appearing in context is **not** permission to retrieve — the proxy is
authoritative. By default a policy allows scoped *search* of the original and
denies wholesale *full* retrieval; both are policy-gated and audited, search is
bounded so it cannot reconstruct the whole original, and an unknown or expired
handle fails closed.

If compression is declared but the original cannot be stored, the run **halts**
with a legible `evidence_error` rather than ever sending compressed-only evidence
to the model.

You bring the policy and (for now) call retrieval from agent code; the model
driving its own retrieval mid-completion arrives with the agentic tool loop.
Durable evidence stores and ML/prose compression are part of the managed service —
the open-source core gives you deterministic transforms, original retention, and
the audited, proxy-scoped retrieval path.

---

# result.status == "halted"

Source: https://github.com/daviesayo/drawbore/blob/main/docs/guide/human-approval.mdx

title: "Human approval"
description: "Resume a gated pipeline with a typed, schema-validated human decision."

**When to use this:** a step marked `requires_human_approval` should pause for a
human, and you want the decision to be a typed, audited artifact — approve, amend,
or reject — not a bare boolean, with the pipeline's safety gates still authoritative
over whatever the human submits.

## Declaring a gated agent

```python
from drawbore import Pipeline, agent
from drawbore.state import InMemoryCheckpointStore

@agent(input=OrderInput, output=RiskScore, requires_human_approval=True)
async def risk_assessor(order: OrderInput) -> RiskScore:
    ...

pipeline = Pipeline()
pipeline.add(risk_assessor)

store = InMemoryCheckpointStore()
```

A gated agent does not have to be model-backed. The `requires_human_approval`
flag applies to any agent — deterministic or model-driven.

## How the two-phase cycle works

A gated step splits execution across two separate `pipeline.run(...)` calls. The
first call produces an `ApprovalRequest` stored in the checkpoint; the second
delivers a typed `ApprovalDecision` and the run continues (or ends, on rejection).

### Phase 1 — run until the gate

```python
result = await pipeline.run(
    initial,
    run_id="order-A-1",
    checkpoints=store,
)
# result.status == "halted"
# result.halt_code == "requires_human_approval"
# result.approval_request is the typed request to hand to a reviewer
request = result.approval_request
print(request.question)         # readable description of what is being asked
print(request.package_legible)  # the full escalation package, as legible text
```

The run halts before executing the gated step. Steps that completed before the
gate are checkpointed; they are not re-executed on the next call.

### Phase 2 — deliver the decision

```python
from drawbore.escalation import ApprovalDecision

# ---- approve as-is ----
decision = ApprovalDecision(
    request_id=request.request_id,
    verdict="approved",
    reviewer_id="alice@example.com",
)

result = await pipeline.run(
    initial,
    run_id="order-A-1",
    checkpoints=store,
    approval=decision,
)
# result.status == "completed" (if no later step halts)
```

```python
# ---- approve with an amendment ----
amended = ApprovalDecision(
    request_id=request.request_id,
    verdict="amended",
    reviewer_id="alice@example.com",
    amended_output={"score": 72, "confidence": 0.91},  # must satisfy the output schema
)

result = await pipeline.run(
    initial,
    run_id="order-A-1",
    checkpoints=store,
    approval=amended,
)
```

```python
# ---- reject ----
rejection = ApprovalDecision(
    request_id=request.request_id,
    verdict="rejected",
    reviewer_id="alice@example.com",
    rationale="Risk score too high for automated approval.",
)

result = await pipeline.run(
    initial,
    run_id="order-A-1",
    checkpoints=store,
    approval=rejection,
)
# result.status == "halted"
# result.halt_code == "approval_rejected"
```

On an approved or amended step, the output is checkpointed and the run continues
from the next step. On rejection the run halts with `halt_code == "approval_rejected"`;
that request is terminal.

The example above uses `InMemoryCheckpointStore`, so a pending request lives only
in process. To let an approval cycle survive a process restart, use a durable
checkpoint store: `FileCheckpointStore(path)` persists the pending request to disk
and a fresh process resumes it (with the decision) without re-executing the gated
agent.

## Invariants

**Schema gate on amendments.** An amended output is validated against the step's
declared output schema exactly as a model output is. If the amendment does not
satisfy the schema the run halts with `halt_code == "schema_violation"` — the
human decision is subject to the same structural check as any other output.

**Approval is not declassification.** An approved or amended output keeps the
trust label of the original execution. If the step produced a tainted output,
that taint is preserved on the checkpointed result; downstream taint and
condition gates see the original trust level. The `proposed_output_trust` field on
the `ApprovalRequest` shows the trust label the output will carry — approving cannot change the trust label: the checkpointed result carries the
join of the original label and the current scope, so UNTRUSTED stays UNTRUSTED.

**Decisions are single-use and request-bound.** An `ApprovalDecision` is
consumed exactly once, matched by `request_id`. Replaying a consumed decision,
or supplying one whose `request_id` does not match the pending request, halts
with `halt_code == "approval_error"`.

**Rejection is terminal for that request.** A rejection ends the pending request.
Re-running the pipeline under the same `run_id` mints a fresh `ApprovalRequest`
so a new decision can be delivered.

**Gated agents should still be idempotent.** The gated agent re-runs only at
first execution (never on a decision-only poll). Write gated agent handlers as
idempotent as a defensive practice — a process restart before the checkpoint is
persisted can cause re-execution.

## Low-confidence steps use the same cycle

A `HasConfidence` step that falls below the pipeline's `confidence_threshold`
resolves through the same approve/amend/reject cycle as an explicit gate, as long
as the run is synchronous and has a checkpoint store. Instead of dying, it mints
an `ApprovalRequest` (with `reason == "confidence_below_threshold"`) and halts
with `halt_code == "confidence_approval_pending"`; deliver an `ApprovalDecision`
the same way to approve, amend (revalidated through the output schema), or reject
it. The human's decision is the resolution of the low confidence — an amended
output that is still below the threshold does not re-trigger the cycle.

Two behaviours are deliberately unchanged. Without a checkpoint store the same
trigger halts terminally as `confidence_below_threshold` (a resume is impossible
without a store). Under an `async` escalation policy the low-confidence trigger
dispatches a review and the run continues, with no resumable request minted.

A step that declares **both** a low confidence and `requires_human_approval`
always goes through the explicit `requires_human_approval` gate, never the
low-confidence cycle — one gate owns the human review, with no bypass.

## Trust boundary

An `approved` audit record asserts that the applied output matches the output
stored in the approval request at halt time. The integrity of that request is the
integrity of the checkpoint store. `InMemoryCheckpointStore` is suitable for
development and single-process flows; for regulated deployments that need durable
or cryptographically signed checkpoints, use a durable store (see
[Durable resume](/guide/durable-resume)).

## Common mistakes

- **Reusing a consumed decision.** Replaying the same `ApprovalDecision` after it
  was already applied halts with `approval_error`. Mint a new decision for the new
  request.
- **Supplying `approval=` without `checkpoints=` and `run_id=`.** The run raises
  `ValueError` immediately — a decision can only apply to a stored request from a
  resumable run.
- **Amending with a payload that does not satisfy the output schema.** The pipeline
  validates the amendment exactly as it validates model output. A non-conforming
  amendment halts with `schema_violation`, not `approval_error`.
- **Treating a rejection as retryable through the same request.** It is not — the
  rejected request is cleared. Re-run the pipeline under the same `run_id` to
  mint a fresh `ApprovalRequest`.

## Related

- [Escalation](/guide/escalation) — how Drawbore builds the escalation package
  and routes it, and the other triggers that stop a run for human input.
- [Durable resume](/guide/durable-resume) — checkpoint stores, cross-process
  resume, and the refuse-on-drift seal that keeps resumed runs consistent.
- [Local testing](/guide/local-testing) — how to mock tools and model responses
  while the real Drawbore safety layer runs end-to-end.
- [Reliability](/guide/reliability) — the full closed vocabulary of
  `halt_code` values, including `approval_rejected` and `approval_error`.
